The gameplay itself can be quite fun. The gunplay in general feels good and satisfying, and plenty of the maps flow well and make for fun, intense engagements. To this day, though, matchmaking is probably some of the worst I've seen in any AAA title. A good 40%-50% of lobbies, since launch, will start populated with bots. These may fill up over time, but there's no reason why a game as large as this has been sees bot-populated lobbies during peak hours.

The constant back-pedaling with promises made during the advertising run prior to release (more grounded and realistic skins, no emphasis on collaborations, etc) is egregious. Certainly better realistic skins compared to recent CoD titles, there are still plenty of weird, unrealistic kits. More and more skins are being released with bright colors, and recently, GLOWING colors. These are, at the end of the day, nitpicks, but still highlight a lack of a consumer-friendly backbone. 
AI-generated skins, models, and emblems, especially with the release of Season 5, also plague the game's marketplace and earnable rewards. That is money siphoned from the actual developers and into the hands of the already-rich CEOs and AI companies. 

I can't in good conscious recommend this game anymore. Dice and EA prove time, and time, and time again that they are spineless entities that do not care about promises made or a positive consumer experience.

You have all the previous battlefield games, codes, mechanics and feedback from players on what was good, great, excellent, bad and terrible, yet you fail to put all of that into a package.

The monetization is also ridiculous. They sold the game (STANDARD EDITION) for 70€ already. Then we get the Battlepass nonsense, skins here and there and other crap. Ridiculous. Back then, for Battlefield 3 and 4, you would gladly start to buy expansion packs to also support the game. Why? Because the games were great and fun. Sure, it also did split up the Playerbase because of people who cannot or did not purchase them and then people who bought this or that pack, would play different maps the standard edition did not have. Now we can also mention the server browser which was amazing back in battlefield 4. A Mechanically Revived Titan Being Cannibalized by Its Own Publisher
One year after its October 2025 launch, Battlefield 6 stands as one of the most frustrating paradoxes in modern PC gaming. On the surface, it was hailed as the grand course correction the franchise desperately needed after the disastrous missteps of Battlefield 2042. And in moments of pure, unscripted squad combat, it genuinely earns that praise. Yet as its first year wraps up with recent Steam user reviews tumbling to a polarizing 50% "Mixed" rating, it is impossible to separate the game's solid mechanical foundation from Electronic Arts' hostile technical policies, creeping live service rot, and a historic $55 billion leveraged buyout that threatens to hollow out the entire company from the inside.
The Nuance: Best in Class Gunplay Meets Creative Hollowing
To give credit where it is due, Battlefield Studios and DICE nailed the kinetic fundamentals of infantry combat. Shooting in Battlefield 6 feels phenomenal. Every weapon class carries distinct weight and mechanical personality: assault rifles demand disciplined burst-fire rhythm, marksman rifles punish rushed follow up shots, and staged partial reloads force split second tactical decisions in the middle of a firefight.
The audiovisual engineering is equally triumphant. Rather than relying on the obnoxious, Vaseline smeared screen blur of past entries, suppression is communicated through visceral acoustic cues and subtle camera shake. Firing a sidearm inside a concrete stairwell produces a sharp, metallic echo that sells the physical scale of the space. Combined with a return to defined class identities and a reactive destruction system where blowing open a load bearing wall isn't a scripted cutscene, but a tactical choice that permanently alters sightlines and cover for the rest of the match the core multiplayer loop Across maps like Cairo, Brooklyn, Gibraltar, and the reworked Golmud Railway can still deliver spectacle no other shooter matches.
However, the cracks appear the moment you look past the physics engine:
 * A Glorified Tech Demo for a Campaign: After a cinematic, rain soaked opening mission that screams big-budget confidence, the six-hour solo campaign collapses into a repetitive corridor slog. The geopolitical plot exists almost entirely as disembodied radio chatter, and the AI is shockingly primitive enemies spawn on predictable timers, sprint blindly into gunfire, or break completely on ladders, while friendly squadmates routinely block doorways and ignore revive prompts.
 * Eroding Identity and Balance: Over its first year of seasonal updates, the grounded military atmosphere promised at launch has increasingly given way to twitchy, Call of Duty chasing pacing. Vehicle combat historically the glue of the Battlefield sandbox suffers from erratic balance swings and handling quirks, while inconsistent netcode frequently leaves firefights feeling like a coin toss.
The Linux Exile: EA Javelin and Unjustified Hostility
Nowhere is EA's anti consumer stubbornness more glaring than in its deliberate lockout of Linux, SteamOS, and Steam Deck players. While the rest of the PC gaming industry has spent the last several years embracing Valve's Proton compatibility layer, EA has doubled down on EA Javelin, its proprietary kernel level anti cheat that mandates Windows, UEFI Secure Boot, and TPM 2.0 while refusing to provide Proton or native Linux support.
EA executives have publicly patted themselves on the back, claiming Javelin has blocked 2.39 million cheat attempts and framing the exclusion of alternative operating systems as a necessary sacrifice for security. That argument collapses under technical scrutiny:
 * Collective Punishment of Legitimate Players: EA didn't just lock Linux users out of Battlefield 6; it retroactively forced Javelin into older legacy titles like Battlefield 1 and Battlefield V, revoking access from paying customers who had been playing those games flawlessly on Linux for years.
 * The Technical Excuse Is Hollow: Treating Linux as an inherently insecure "cheater haven" ignores reality. Modern Linux distributions can utilize UEFI Secure Boot with custom signing keys and verify system integrity through TPM attestations in user space without turning the operating system kernel into a proprietary black box rootkit. Furthermore, competitors have long supported user space anti cheat modules inside Proton with minimal friction.
 * Security Theater vs. Hardware Cheats: For all of EA's insistence on invasive ring-0 kernel access on Windows, serious cheat developers didn't stop they simply moved to Direct Memory Access (DMA) PCIe hardware cards with spoofed device firmware that read memory externally, bypassing software kernel checks while legitimate Linux and handheld PC gamers are left out in the cold.
The $55 Billion Guillotine: How EA's Buyout Spells Its Downfall
If Battlefield 6's post launch trajectory already felt increasingly predatory, the corporate seismic shift that closed on August 4, 2026, explains why the worst is still ahead. In the largest leveraged buyout (LBO) in corporate history, EA was taken private in a $55 billion ($210-per-share) deal by a consortium consisting of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (holding roughly 93.4%), private equity giant Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners.
To understand why this buyout is an existential threat to EA's studios and franchises, you only have to look at the balance sheet math:
 * Crushing Debt Placed on EA's Own Books: In a leveraged buyout, the buyers use the target company's own assets as collateral. To fund the takeover, roughly $18 billion to $20 billion in high-yield debt (with bonds priced between 6.25% and 8.75%) was dumped directly onto EA's balance sheet.
 * Interest Payments Exceed Profits: Servicing that debt requires roughly $1.8 billion per year in interest payments alone. In its prior fiscal year, EA generated $887 million in net income. In short, servicing the debt used to buy EA now costs significantly more every year than the company actually earned in profit.
 * Layoffs and "Organizational Efficiencies": Because the debt must be repaid out of EA's operating cash flow, the gutting started immediately. EA executed three separate rounds of layoffs in February, March, and June 2026 before the deal even officially closed, and subsequently promised debt investors $700 million in annual cost cuts, including $170 million in "organizational efficiencies" corporate speak for mass studio layoffs, alongside aggressive mandates to replace human creative workflows with generative AI.
When a publisher is saddled with $20 billion in debt and stripped of development staff, margin expansion can only come from one place: squeezing existing players dry. Battlefield 6 has already become the testing ground for this desperation. Players who already paid full price for the base game are bombarded with prompts for a $24.99 cash-only "Battlefield Pro" tier (which cannot even be bought with earned in-game currency) that gates basic community infrastructure—like hosting 100 player persistent Portal servers behind a recurring paywall. Prior to Season 3, EA even began pushing $24.99 Battle Pass pre-orders before announcing what items were actually inside the pass a move that solves zero problems for players, existing purely to pull revenue forward for debt ridden financial reporting.
The Verdict
Battlefield 6 proves that the engineers and artists at Battlefield Studios still know how to build a thunderous, tactile military sandbox. The gunplay, soundscape, and environmental destruction deserve a spot alongside the franchise's golden era peaks.
Yet it is impossible to wholeheartedly recommend a game whose publisher treats Linux users like criminals, locks community server capabilities behind multi tiered subscription passes, and is now chained to an $18+ billion private-equity debt bomb. Battlefield 6 isn't dying because of the developers. It's EA.

A Worthy Successor to Battlefield 4 and Battlefield V

Recommended 👍
After playing Battlefield 4 and Battlefield V, Battlefield 6 is the next Battlefield game that has really caught my attention. The gunplay feels great, the shooting mechanics are satisfying, and the overall gameplay has that Battlefield feel that makes the series so enjoyable.

The graphics are pretty nice too, and the visuals help make the battles feel immersive. The gunplay is definitely one of the biggest highlights for me. Weapons feel good to use, and getting into firefights is genuinely fun.
Coming from Battlefield 4 and Battlefield V, I'm happy with what Battlefield 6 brings to the table. It feels like a solid addition to the franchise, and I've been enjoying my time with it.
My only major complaint so far is the matchmaking. Finding a match can take longer than it should, which gets frustrating when all you want to do is jump into the action. Hopefully, this gets improved in future updates.
Overall, I'm having a great time with Battlefield 6. The gunplay is excellent, the graphics look good, and the core Battlefield experience is enjoyable. Fix the matchmaking issues, and this could be an even better experience.
Verdict: Recommended. If you're a Battlefield fan, especially if you've enjoyed BF4 and BFV, Battlefield 6 is worth checking out. See you on the battlefield! 🎮

review: Good to be back

Battlefield 6 abandons everything that made this franchise great and desperately chases Call of Duty's style until it breaks. The fast pacing is completely overdone, and the mandatory slide mechanics make every encounter feel cheap and unstrategic. Gunfights aren't won by positioning or tactics anymore because everybody can be heard like they're an elephant.

The marketing and "cool" aesthetic can’t hide the fact that the core gameplay lacks FUN and identity. There’s no weight to the shooting, no satisfaction in conquering a map together, and no room for the chaotic, unpredictable moments that made old Battlefield legendary. It’s clear where DICE’s priorities lie: engagement metrics and wallet extraction over player experience.
Every single Battlefield game does it better than this one. A completely unfortunate regression of the series filled with ridiculous cosmetic slop.

[b]By now they removed multiple gamemodes, including: Rush (one of the all time favorite modes of the Battlefield community), Air Superiority, Carrier Assault, Squad Deathmatch, Strikepoint and the list goes on.[/b] They added various vehicles that are tied to certain maps only, e.g. the two seater F18.

One of EA's biggest promises before the release in 2025 was to "keep the player skins grounded and realistic". Not even a year in and we got glowing, ember-like uniforms on characters, saturated blue "camouflage"  and a bright green slime inspired skin (which admittedly they fixed/removed by now).

It's a shame honestly that this comes from the same studio that once put so much love into titles like Battlefield 1, 3 or 4.
